title: Not quite eye to A.I.: student and teacher perspectives on the use of generative artificial intelligence in the writing process
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines how university students and teachers perceive the acceptable use of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, across different stages of the writing process. The core problem is that generative AI can support writing in useful ways but also creates new concerns around plagiarism, authorship, academic integrity, and appropriate classroom use. The study asks what students and teachers think about using generative AI for brainstorming, outlining, writing, revising, feedback, and evaluation, and how those perspectives compare.

The authors used a cross-sectional questionnaire survey. Participants were shown examples of prompts and outputs from ChatGPT for six writing-related tasks, then asked to rate the appropriateness of four different forms of use: using AI when already competent at the task, using AI output as a model for ideas, submitting AI-generated output with disclosure, and submitting AI-generated output without disclosure. The study therefore did not test an instructional intervention for learning outcomes, but rather investigated perceptions of possible AI-supported practices in writing education.

The sample included 226 participants: 158 students and 68 teachers. Students were mainly undergraduates from a public research university in the United States, with a small number of graduate students. Teachers were recruited from multiple institutions worldwide, though most were adult/university instructors and many were English language teachers; the largest teacher subgroup was in the United States, followed by China and other countries. The context is higher education and adult teaching, focused on writing instruction and assessment.

The main conclusion is that students and teachers broadly agreed on a normative boundary: using generative AI for idea generation, modeling, or support in early writing stages was more acceptable, while submitting AI-produced writing or teacher-generated AI feedback/evaluation without disclosure was generally viewed as inappropriate. Students were somewhat more permissive than teachers about undisclosed student use, while teachers were somewhat more accepting of using AI as a model for feedback and evaluation. The paper also concludes that institutions and classrooms were largely unprepared for generative AI, with very limited policy guidance or training reported, leading the authors to recommend explicit guidelines, transparency, and professional development for educators.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's chatbot interface to GPT-family large language models that generates and revises text and can provide feedback or evaluative comments on writing.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate example prompts and outputs for six writing-process tasks (brainstorming, outlining, writing, revising, feedback, evaluating) that were shown in a survey comparing student and teacher perceptions of acceptable use.

findings.finding_summary: In a cross-sectional survey, students (n=158) and teachers (n=68) generally agreed that ChatGPT use was more acceptable for idea generation/modeling than for completing and submitting writing tasks. Significant group differences appeared on several items: for brainstorming without disclosure, students were more accepting than teachers (U=4491, r=-0.143, p=0.032); for outlining, students were more accepting on using output as a model (U=3949.5, r=-0.217, p=0.001), submitting with disclosure (U=4488.5, r=-0.134, p<0.05), and without disclosure (U=3973.5, p<0.001); for writing, students were more accepting of submitting AI-written essays with disclosure (U=4311.5, r=-0.169, p=0.011) and without disclosure (U=4245.5, r=-0.223, p<0.001).
findings.measure: Survey ratings of appropriateness of ChatGPT use across writing-process tasks and disclosure conditions
findings.effect_size: r=-0.143 to -0.223 on significant between-group comparisons

findings.finding_summary: For revision tasks, students were more accepting than teachers of submitting ChatGPT-revised writing with disclosure (U=4393, r=-0.15, p<0.05) and without disclosure (U=4030, r=-0.23, p<0.001), though the majority of both groups still viewed these uses as inappropriate. For teacher-oriented uses, teachers were more accepting than students of using ChatGPT-generated feedback as a model (U=6397, r=-0.157, p<0.05) and ChatGPT-generated evaluation as a model (U=6247, r=-0.133, p<0.05).
findings.measure: Survey ratings of appropriateness of ChatGPT for revision, feedback, and evaluation tasks
findings.effect_size: r=-0.133 to -0.23 on significant between-group comparisons

findings.finding_summary: Both groups reported substantial institutional unpreparedness for ChatGPT/AI use. Among students, 52% reported their university had an AI policy and 47% said it did not; among teachers, only 5.9% reported their institution had a policy and 94.1% said it did not. About 94.3% of students and 95.6% of teachers reported receiving no institutional training on AI, and 89.7% of teachers reported they had not educated their students about appropriate AI use.
findings.measure: Yes/no survey items on AI policy, training, and classroom guidance

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical cross-sectional survey study of perceptions, not an RCT or quasi-experimental effectiveness study. It provides systematic primary evidence about attitudes and institutional readiness, but causal impact on learning outcomes is not established.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report direct learning-effect effect sizes or achievement gains; impacts are mainly perceptual and institutional, with mixed attitudes and clear evidence of low preparedness. Because outcome impact on student learning is unclear, the impact tier is yellow.
